query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid free‐energy method that replaces full-length ab initio molecular dynamics with a two‐stage approach—first, running very short AIMD simulations to extract vibrational covariance matrices (which retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling) to parameterize an effective force-constant model, and then training a machine-learning (e.g., moment-tensor potential) surrogate that rapidly samples both solid and liquid configuration spaces—can yield accurate fusion free energies for high-temperature and multicomponent (high-entropy) systems at a fraction of the computational cost of explicit AIMD or TOR‐TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: A representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy (HEA) system in its near-melting (solid) state and its corresponding liquid state under fusion-relevant high-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Replace the full-length explicit AIMD free-energy evaluation with a hybrid approach: (1) run short AIMD simulations to compute vibrational displacement covariances (thus capturing key anharmonic and electron–vibration effects) for both solid and fluid phases; (2) use these data to fit an effective, ML-based interatomic potential that can be used in fast Monte Carlo or short-dynamics sampling to compute complete free-energy landscapes.
generation.conditions: Simulations are performed across the temperature range near the melting point (fusion conditions) and over a compositional window extending from binary to multi-component high-entropy alloys. Controlled variables include simulation cell size, short AIMD trajectory length sufficient for converging covariance measures, and an ML training error threshold that ensures retention of vibrational and anharmonic details.
generation.structural_mediator: The vibrational covariance matrix derived from short AIMD acts as the mediator to encapsulate the relevant entropy contributions and anharmonic interactions. These are then embedded into the ML surrogate potential, which mediates the efficient evaluation of free energies for both phases.
generation.mechanism: By capturing the essential physics—vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling—from short AIMD runs using a Gaussian approximation and then leveraging the efficiency of a trained ML potential to sample the free-energy landscape, the method approximates the complete phase free energies without requiring extended MD trajectories. This preserves the fidelity of the entropy terms while substantially reducing computational expense, especially in complex, multicomponent systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is predicted to compute phase free energies (and derived fusion observables such as melting point and latent heat) with fidelity comparable to explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD for elemental/binary systems, but with an order-of-magnitude speedup in high-entropy, multicomponent alloys.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio MD free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD workflows, which are highly accurate for elemental and binary systems but become prohibitively slow for complex, multicomponent alloys.
generation.boundary: The approach is targeted at systems where the vibrational amplitudes remain moderate (so that the Gaussian covariance approximation is valid) and for temperature ranges near fusion (melting) conditions. It is applicable from simpler binary alloys up to high-entropy alloys with five or more principal elements.
generation.uncertainty: While initial elemental and binary benchmarks (as seen in prior vibrational entropy studies) are promising, the ability of the ML surrogate to faithfully reproduce electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic effects in high-entropy systems remains to be fully validated. The generality across different alloy chemistries and the limits of the Gaussian approximation introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform benchmark calculations on a well-characterized binary alloy (e.g., Al or a Ni-based system) and on a representative high-entropy alloy. For each, compute the phase free energy difference between the solid and liquid states using (a) the conventional full-length AIMD (or TOR-TILD) method and (b) the proposed hybrid method. Ensure that simulation parameters (cell size, temperature, pressure) are identical.
measurements: Absolute free energy of solid and liquid phases
Fusion observables such as melting point and latent heat
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the free energy differences or derived fusion observables (melting point, latent heat) computed via the hybrid method deviate by more than an acceptable error margin (e.g., >5–10%) from those obtained via full AIMD/TOR-TILD, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The method applies generally to solids, but the particular implementation given here relies on the accuracy of a Gaussian approximation to the distribution function. Hence it is most likely to work when the atomic displacements are small, and it is likely to fail in molecular solids where coherent bond rotations are present. Although we mainly demonstrated the method for elemental solids, it also holds in principle for complex crystalline and noncrystalline solids. We give an example of such an application for the MoNbTaW high entropy alloy. The quasiharmonic method may be equally accurate and more efficient than our AIMD method when anharmonicity mainly enters through thermal expansion, but a simulation-based approach in principle includes additional anharmonic contributions. Doing so may require correlations beyond those captured by the Gaussian approximation (see Section 3.3.1). Our simulation-based approach seems most useful when the simulation has already been completed for other purposes. Then, the entropy comes essentially for free on top of whatever other information was sought.
